title: Stack & Queue Fundamentals
summary: LIFO vs FIFO mechanics and how each is actually implemented over an array or linked list — the two access disciplines every stack and queue problem builds on.

slides.markdown:
A **stack** only lets you touch the most recently added item — last in, first out. A **queue** only lets you touch the oldest item still waiting — first in, first out. That's the entire interface difference, and yet it determines which real-world problems each one solves.

Undo history, function call stacks, and matching nested brackets are all naturally LIFO. Task scheduling, breadth-first search, and print queues are all naturally FIFO. Recognizing which discipline a problem statement is describing — often without saying "stack" or "queue" out loud — is the actual skill this group builds toward.

Both can be implemented over either a dynamic array or a linked list; the choice affects performance in specific, testable ways covered here.

slides.subTitle: What moves where
slides.markdown:
A stack has one active end: pushes and pops both happen at the top. A queue has two active ends: enqueue happens at the back (tail), dequeue happens at the front (head).

slides.subTitle: Resizing cost vs pointer overhead
slides.markdown:
| | Array-backed | Linked-list-backed |
|---|---|---|
| Push/enqueue | amortized O(1) (occasional resize) | O(1), no resize ever |
| Memory overhead | none per element | one+ pointer per element |
| Cache behavior | excellent | poor |
| Fixed max size option | natural (pre-allocate) | needs an explicit counter |

An array-backed stack or queue occasionally pays an O(n) resize when it outgrows its backing buffer, but that cost amortizes to O(1) per operation over the buffer's lifetime — the same argument used for dynamic array append. A linked-list-backed version never resizes, at the cost of a pointer per node and worse cache locality.

In practice, most language standard libraries back their stack/queue/deque types with a resizable array (or a circular buffer, next slide) rather than a linked list, precisely because of the cache argument.

slides.sectionTitle: Implementing a stack with a dynamic array
slides.subTitle: push, pop, peek

slides.sectionTitle: Popping or peeking an empty stack
slides.subTitle: Without checking first
slides.markdown:
```python
# BUG: assumes the stack is non-empty
def pop(self):
    return self._data.pop()  # raises on empty, or worse: silently
                              # returns a sentinel that looks valid
```

The safe version explicitly checks emptiness and raises (or returns a clearly-invalid sentinel documented as such) rather than letting the underlying array's own error propagate confusingly, or — worse — returning `None` in a context where `None` is also a legitimate stored value, making "empty" indistinguishable from "top element is None."

This matters most in composite algorithms (monotonic stack, expression evaluation) where an empty-stack pop is often a **valid signal** — "there's no matching opening bracket" — that the calling code needs to detect and act on, not something that should crash deep inside a helper method.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a naive array queue wastes space
slides.markdown:
If you implement a queue by enqueuing at the back (`append`) and dequeuing at the front (`pop(0)` or shifting every remaining element left by one), dequeue costs O(n) — every remaining element has to move.

Even avoiding that shift by just advancing a "front index" pointer instead of physically moving elements creates a different problem: the space **before** the front index is now permanently wasted, since nothing is ever placed back there. After enough enqueue/dequeue cycles, you can have a nearly-empty logical queue sitting inside an array that's still consuming its full original allocation, all in the unused prefix.

Both failure modes — the O(n) shift and the wasted prefix — point at the same fix: treat the backing array as **circular**, wrapping indices around instead of always growing forward.

slides.sectionTitle: Implementing a queue with a circular buffer
slides.markdown:
```python
class CircularQueue:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self._buf = [None] * capacity
        self._cap = capacity
        self._front = 0
        self._size = 0

    def enqueue(self, x):
        if self._size == self._cap:
            raise OverflowError("queue full")
        idx = (self._front + self._size) % self._cap
        self._buf[idx] = x
        self._size += 1

    def dequeue(self):
        if self._size == 0:
            raise IndexError("queue empty")
        x = self._buf[self._front]
        self._front = (self._front + 1) % self._cap
        self._size -= 1
        return x
```

Both enqueue and dequeue are O(1), and the buffer's used space never grows unboundedly — the `% self._cap` wraps indices back to the start once they run past the end, reusing the prefix space a naive implementation would waste.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading a problem for its LIFO/FIFO signal
slides.markdown:
| Phrase in the problem | Signal | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| "most recently", "undo", "nested", "matching pairs" | last in, first out | stack |
| "in the order received", "level by level", "first come first served" | first in, first out | queue |
| "next greater/smaller", "valid parentheses" | LIFO with a twist | stack |
| "shortest path", "minimum steps", "spreading outward" | FIFO with a twist | queue (BFS) |

Most problems don't say "use a stack" outright — they describe an access pattern, and recognizing which discipline that pattern matches is the transferable skill. "Undo the last N actions" is a stack even though the word never appears; "process requests in arrival order with fairness" is a queue for the same reason.

slides.sectionTitle: Using list.pop(0) as a queue dequeue
slides.subTitle: Silently paying O(n)
slides.markdown:
```python
queue = []
queue.append(x)      # O(1) — fine
front = queue.pop(0)  # BUG: O(n) — every remaining element shifts left
```

Many languages' plain dynamic-array list type only makes `pop()` from the **end** O(1); `pop(0)` (or any `pop(i)` for i != last) requires shifting every subsequent element down by one slot, an O(n) operation dressed up as a single method call. Code that looks like a clean O(1) queue can silently be O(n) per dequeue — and O(n²) total over a full run — with no obvious warning sign in the code itself.

The fix is to use a structure actually designed for both-end O(1) access — a deque (Python's `collections.deque`, Java's `ArrayDeque`) — rather than a plain array-backed list used as if it supported cheap front removal.

Stack and queue are the simplest possible data structures — an array or list with a restricted interface — but that restriction is the entire point. Restricting *where* you're allowed to touch the structure is what gives push/pop or enqueue/dequeue their O(1) guarantee: you never have to search for the right position, because the interface only ever offers you one.

This is a pattern that recurs throughout the rest of this group and beyond: monotonic stacks, sliding-window deques, and priority queues are all built by adding a single extra invariant on top of this same restricted-access idea, rather than replacing it with something more complex.
